arguments.name: Minimal facts consensus is not merely Christian bias
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The scholarly consensus on the minimal facts for the resurrection is not undermined by the fact that many scholars who accept them are Christians, because non-Christian and skeptical scholars also accept them.
premises: P1: The Jesus Seminar, which dedicated its work to skeptics like David Hume and Thomas Jefferson and praised David Strauss, still admits many of the minimal facts.
P2: James D. G. Dunn, who held a non-orthodox christological view, can be found affirming the six facts repeatedly.
P3: Antony Flew, the world's best-known philosophical atheist at the time, accepted all twelve facts in a debate with Habermas.
P4: If Christian bias were the explanation, the empty tomb would be a minimal fact, but many Christians deny it because they follow the data.

st1.quote: Sure, you've got the scholarly consensus, but take a look at the Society of Biblical Literature or, you know, the EPS or something. The The vast majority of those scholars are already Christians and therefore they're committed to that.

st2.quote: And the two volumes the two major volumes put up by the Jesus Seminar. Now, I'm not going to argue whether they are Christians or not Christians, but when they de- uh devote their book to people like David Hume, Thomas Jefferson who took scissors and paste to the Gospels.

st3.quote: Tony Flew as far as I know when he was an atheist had no problems with the minimal facts. In fact, we started one of the three debates. I put 12 facts up.

st4.quote: But no, Gary's research and and scholarship has shown that no, they're being honest to the data, right? Because if if that was true, then the empty tomb would be a minimal fact.

st5.quote: So, they'll just say, "Well, that's a bi- it's a bias in that the sample no one uh Christians are going to agree with your minimal facts to begin with.

st6.quote: And then what are they going to say? Oh, isn't he your fellow professor at Liberty University? I mean, you know, they'll try to they'll try to squeeze anything to anything

st8.quote: I can find my six facts over and over and over and over and over in James D. G. Dunn. And then what are they going to say? ... Tony Flew as far as I know when he was an atheist had no problems with the minimal facts.

or1.quote: One of the number one objections, not just to you, but to to anytime a minimal facts approach is brought up, it's it's an objection I've always heard
or1.why: This is Habermas's own long-running defense of the minimal-facts method, restated in interview form against the standard bias objection.

or2.quote: the two major volumes put up by the Jesus Seminar. Now, I'm not going to argue whether they are Christians or not Christians, but when they de- uh devote their book to people like David Hume, Thomas Jefferson who took scissors and paste to the Gospels.
or2.why: Adds the Jesus Seminar's own dedication to Hume/Jefferson/Strauss and the Flew 12-facts anecdote as specific supporting data.

or3.why: No cross-domain connection is made; the argument stays within historical-critical scholarship.

or4.why: No formalization, model or structure is introduced.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas & Michael Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, 2004
arguments.weakest_link: P3 (Flew's acceptance of all 12 facts) rests on Habermas's recollection of a debate rather than a citable published statement.
arguments.develop_next: Cite the exact debate transcript/date and Flew's own words accepting the 12 facts, plus a published Jesus Seminar volume page for the minimal facts.

arguments.name: Even radical critics like Bultmann support early sources
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Even Rudolf Bultmann, a very liberal scholar, affirms key historical data such as a pre-Markan passion narrative and early Jerusalem church sayings, which strengthens the case for the minimal facts.
premises: P1: Bultmann is listed among critical scholars who accept a pre-Markan passion narrative that may predate AD 37.
P2: Bultmann says the early sayings go back to the very earliest Jerusalem church.
P3: In his 1941 essay, Bultmann states that the earliest disciples preached that Jesus was raised from the dead.
P4: Bultmann is to the left of Bart Ehrman and does not like historical backup for faith, yet he still concedes these points.

st2.quote: Bultmann's name is in that list, and he doesn't accept a whole lot of the verses, but he says there was a Markan pre-Markan narrative, and he only uses a few verses.

st3.quote: Also, in his 1941 essay, uh New Testament Mythology, the very famous thing that got rolling toward demythologization, uh Bultmann says, "What can we say about the um aftermath of the cross?" He says, "The earliest disciples preached that he was raised from the dead."

st4.quote: Guess what Rudolf Bultmann says, way to the left. He says, "These early sayings go back to the very earliest Jerusalem church."

st5.quote: And he lists a bunch of critical scholars who think that Mark did use a source that some say, and I won't give the reasons, but that some say predates 37 AD.

st6.quote: That's Bultmann, very earliest. If you If you know what I'm Look, these people aren't in the book because I generally don't go back to the to 1941 for sources, but you can find these guys.

st8.quote: In the back of Raymond Brown's two-volume The Death of the Messiah ... he's reproduced Soards' essay on the pre-Markan passion narrative. And he lists a bunch of critical scholars who think that Mark did use a source

or1.quote: Bultmann's name is in that list, and he doesn't accept a whole lot of the verses, but he says there was a Markan pre-Markan narrative
or1.why: A variant of Habermas's standing appeal to hostile-witness concessions, here focused on Bultmann's source-critical admissions.

or2.quote: In the back of Raymond Brown's two-volume The Death of the Messiah ... he's reproduced Soards' essay on the pre-Markan passion narrative.

arguments.name: Christian scholars debate the evidence, not just assume resurrection
arguments.speaker: Bill (co-host)
arguments.conclusion: The fact that many scholars are Christians does not mean they simply assume the resurrection; they debate the evidence and reach conclusions based on data.
premises: P1: If Christian bias determined conclusions, the empty tomb would be a minimal fact, but many Christians deny it.
P2: The quotes in Habermas's volumes show scholars debating the evidence rather than merely asserting Christian beliefs.
P3: The strong consensus on the six minimal facts stems from the strength of the data, not from shared faith.

st4.quote: It's because even though they're Christians, they're basing their conclusions on the data. And the data is so strong in the case of your six minimal facts, that's why there is that strong consensus.

st6.quote: That alone says nothing about their conclusions about the minimal facts because you can see from the quotes in there, they're debating the evidence.

st8.quote: Because if if that was true, then the empty tomb would be a minimal fact. Not You know, if if they're all just a bunch of Christians, why on earth are Christians denying the empty tomb?

arguments.name: Bultmann himself calls resurrection a myth
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Bultmann explicitly dismisses the resurrection as a myth, showing that even a scholar who accepts some historical data rejects the resurrection itself.
premises: P1: In his 1941 essay, Bultmann begins a section on the resurrection by asking, 'Is it not a myth pure and simple?'
P2: Bultmann does not weigh pros and cons; he already treats it as a myth that did not happen.

st1.quote: He starts a section out called the resurrection. And here's the first thing he says. And what about the resurrection? {question mark} Is it not a myth pure and simple? {question mark}

st2.quote: And then he doesn't say, well, let's do the pros and cons. No, he's done with it. He's already said it's a myth. It didn't happen.

st3.quote: By the way, here's here's Bultmann's quote. It is 1941 essay. I'm only going to miss this by a word or two.

st4.quote: He's already said it's a myth. It didn't happen.

st6.quote: He's already said it's a myth. It didn't happen.

or1.quote: Is it not a myth pure and simple? {question mark} And then he doesn't say, well, let's do the pros and cons.

arguments.name: Scholarly consensus should target informed scholars who publish
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: A scholarly consensus argument should focus on scholars who have published in the field of resurrection research because they have informed opinions, not on all PhDs regardless of expertise.
premises: P1: Scholars like Bethany Hughes have a PhD in history but have never published on resurrection research, so their opinion is uninformed.
P2: We want people who have actually studied the resurrection research and published an opinion.
P3: Habermas defines a critical scholar as one with a terminal degree who has worked in a relevant area such as New Testament, Old Testament, history, philosophy, archaeology, or world religions.
P4: He allows exceptions for people without terminal degrees who know the data, such as G. A. Wells, but generally requires publication or public scholarly engagement.

st1.quote: how can you make a scholarly consensus argument if you're not interviewing all scholars, only the subset who publish in the literature.

st2.quote: when I say I I say a critical scholar ha- it I this is defined in volume one in particular has the following uh characteristics. They have a terminal degree.

st3.quote: Bethany Hughes, she she has a PhD in history, she she's quali- she does a bunch of BBC documentaries. If you want to know the history of Socrates, she's great, but she doesn't know anything about resurrection research. She's never published anything.

st4.quote: the reason you target the ones that are publishing is because we when we have a scholarly consensus, we want it to be an informed group of scholars.

st5.quote: some skeptics say, well, how can you make a scholarly consensus argument if you're not interviewing all scholars, only the subset who publish in the literature.

st6.quote: They have a terminal degree. Now, we usually think of that as a PhD, but in in England and Europe, they have different letters.

st8.quote: I also allow history, historians, philosophers, people with doctorates in archaeology, believe it or not. ... Somebody I would accept somebody with a PhD in world religions.

or1.quote: when I say I I say a critical scholar ha- it I this is defined in volume one in particular has the following uh characteristics.
or1.why: A methodological variant within Habermas's own program, spelling out the critical-scholar criteria.

or2.quote: G. A. Wells, yeah, he had a PhD in German. I I I wouldn't call that in somebody in a field, but I cite him cuz he knows how to do research.
or2.why: Adds the Wells exception and the list of accepted fields as concrete selection data.

or4.quote: They have a terminal degree. ... I say, I'll I would accept New Testament. I even say, I will accept Old Testament.
or4.why: Offers an explicit eligibility rule (terminal degree + relevant field + publication) that can be applied as a criterion.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Risen Jesus and Future Hope / minimal-facts volumes, 2003
arguments.weakest_link: The claim that publication guarantees an 'informed opinion' is a proxy that is asserted rather than validated.
arguments.develop_next: Show empirically that published resurrection scholars agree on the six facts at a much higher rate than non-publishing PhDs, so the selection rule is defensible.

arguments.name: Habermas is deliberately lenient toward liberal scholars
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Habermas's selection criteria are biased in favor of liberal scholars, not conservative ones, because he wants to include critics and give everyone a fair shot.
premises: P1: He states at the beginning of his book that he is slanted toward liberal scholars.
P2: He includes scholars like Bultmann who are far to the left and not conservative in almost anything.
P3: He makes allowances for people who do not meet his criteria, such as 19th-century German philosophers without terminal degrees, because they are well-known for certain views.
P4: Critics who question his fairness are not reading the data carefully.

st1.quote: I do say I am slanted toward liberal scholars. And you go, "Well, that's not you. I know where you teach." Well, you're you're not listening to my nuance.

st2.quote: I really do think I I'm more lenient with liberals than I am with conservatives because I want to put people in there who don't have all the training, but I want to be honest giving everybody a shot.

st3.quote: Almost none of those German philosophers 19th century have earned doctorates, have terminal degrees in their field. But they did a lot of research in those days and and and they did these things. So I I approve even if I can't stand maybe what they're saying.

st4.quote: I'm more lenient with liberals than I am with conservatives because I want to put people in there who don't have all the training

st5.quote: And people who question me on that, they're they're not being fair with reading through the data.

st6.quote: So so in a way it's prejudiced, if you call this prejudice, in favor of those who have written on this topic.

st8.quote: I get I get attacked so often by the so-called Jesus mythers. "Why don't you allow us?" ... I make a little allowance here and there

or1.quote: I do say I am slanted toward liberal scholars.
or1.why: A variant of Habermas's own recurring self-description of his selection policy.

or2.quote: Almost none of those German philosophers 19th century have earned doctorates, have terminal degrees in their field. But they did a lot of research in those days
or2.why: Adds the 19th-century German philosophers and the Wells case as evidence of deliberate leniency.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus, 1996 (preface on slant toward critical scholars)
arguments.weakest_link: The evidence for leniency is Habermas's own self-report, with no independent audit of who was included or excluded.
arguments.develop_next: Publish the full inclusion/exclusion list with each scholar's theological position so the liberal slant can be independently checked.

arguments.name: Jesus Seminar presupposes that dead men do not rise
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The Jesus Seminar's rejection of resurrection sayings is based on a presupposition that dead men do not rise, which is a weak starting point for historical study.
premises: P1: The Jesus Seminar lists 38 or 39 presuppositions at the beginning of volume one.
P2: One presupposition states that people wonder why they have no words from the resurrected Jesus in the Gospels, and the reason is 'Dead men don't rise.'
P3: They conclude that Jesus's life ends on Good Friday evening.
P4: This is a massive presupposition that simply assumes the point at issue.

st1.quote: They say, "People wonder why we don't have any words that are purported from the resurrected Jesus in the Gospels. There's a reason for it. Dead men don't rise. And so for us, his life ends on Good Friday evening."

st2.quote: Go to the beginning of volume one of their two and they have 30-something, 38, 39 presuppositions with which they wrote these things.

st3.quote: Go to the beginning of volume one of their two and they have 30-something, 38, 39 presuppositions with which they wrote these things.

st4.quote: I think that's kind of weak.

st5.quote: I'm not going to argue whether they are Christians or not Christians

st6.quote: I think that's kind of weak.

st8.quote: Go to the beginning of volume one of their two and they have 30-something, 38, 39 presuppositions with which they wrote these things.

or1.quote: Go to the beginning of volume one of their two and they have 30-something, 38, 39 presuppositions with which they wrote these things.
or1.why: It is a variant of Habermas's standing critique of the Jesus Seminar's naturalistic presuppositions, here pointed at a specific numbered presupposition.

or2.quote: They say, "People wonder why we don't have any words that are purported from the resurrected Jesus in the Gospels. There's a reason for it. Dead men don't rise. And so for us, his life ends on Good Friday evening."
or2.why: It quotes the Seminar's own listed presupposition directly, which the prior art does not use.

or3.why: No cross-domain connection is made; the argument stays within historical-critical method.

or4.why: No formalization, model, or equation is added.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (ancient evidence for the historical Jesus), 1996
arguments.weakest_link: P4: the charge that the presupposition 'assumes the point at issue' is asserted rather than argued, since the Seminar could claim it is a methodological default to be overturned by evidence.
arguments.develop_next: Quote the presupposition verbatim with volume and page so it can be checked, then show why a methodological default differs from a conclusion.

arguments.name: Mythicists are not qualified to be included
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Jesus mythicists are not included in the scholarly consensus because they lack relevant credentials and are rejected even by critical scholars like Bart Ehrman.
premises: P1: Bart Ehrman devotes 20 pages in The Evidence for Jesus to explaining why mythicists do not line up with scholarship.
P2: Ehrman says mythicists have all their sources but are the only ones who have them, and nobody likes them.
P3: One mythicist claims a PhD and expertise in ancient subjects but has no college degrees.
P4: Habermas makes allowances for people without PhDs who know the data, but not for those who lack relevant expertise.

st5.quote: I would I make allowances for people who don't have PhDs, but who know the data.
